title: Can Dell Stock Fall 40%?
detail:
Can Dell Stock Fall 40%?
Trefis Team

DELL
^GSPC
HPQ
HPE
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Dell Technologies (DELL) stock has experienced 40% drops before. During three of the seven market shocks since the shares began trading in December 2018, the stock fell 40% or more from its peak in the shock to its eventual low. On November 12, 2026, the shares closed 36.8% below their September high. They lost 26.8% over the past month, compared with a 1.6% dip for the S&P 500, with no earnings report released in that time. So how deep did Dell's falls in past shocks run against the market, and how long did the stock take to get back?

How Deep Did Dell Fall, And For How Long?

Dell's deepest fall in a market shock occurred during the 2020 COVID-19 crash, when the stock lost 46% compared to 34% for the market, measured by the SPY S&P 500 fund. Across all seven shocks, Dell fell 27.1% on average from the first day of each shock to its low, nearly twice the fund's 14.5%. Its largest fall since 2018 spanned from May 2024 to April 2025 and took 59.6% off the stock.

Dell has usually reclaimed its previous highs within months. Measured from the low, the median recovery took 2.7 months, and the stock ultimately returned to its peak after all seven shocks. The longest wait occurred following the shock of summer 2024, when Dell needed 13.8 months to return to its high.

Dell Now Turns More Revenue Into Profit

So far, Dell's fast growth has coincided with a wider operating margin. Revenue reached $151 billion over the twelve months ending July 31, 2026, climbing 49.0% from a year earlier. Operating margin over those months rose to 9.6% from 7.1% a year earlier, reaching the highest twelve-month level across any of the 40 quarter-ends since fiscal Q3 2017.

Gross margin moved the other way, slipping to 19.8% from 21.1% over the same months. Management credits scale for the wider operating margin, and said operating expenses, on an adjusted basis, fell to 8.5% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2027.

The Infrastructure Solutions Group, which houses Dell's servers and storage, generated $60.8 billion in fiscal 2026, an increase of 39.5%. This growth pushed the unit ahead of the Client Solutions Group, the PC business, which had been the larger of the two a year earlier. Total debt expanded alongside the business operations, reaching $34.5 billion at the end of July 2026, up from $28.7 billion a year earlier.

Dell Faces Parts Shortages And Thinner PC Profit

Dell cannot secure all the parts its customers want, management said on the September 1, 2026 call. The company identified DRAM, followed by NAND, as the tightest constraints, alongside spotty CPU shortages. Traditional server and networking revenue rose 122% to $10.5 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, and management said demand still outpaced supply. Management said Dell's input costs keep going up, and that part of the server growth came from price increases.

Key Takeaways

ADP raised its quarterly dividend 12% on Nov. 11, its 52nd consecutive year of increases, while IBM declared its regular $1.69 quarterly dividend on Oct. 21.

IBM yields 2.7% to ADP's 2.4%, and its dividend took a smaller share of free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 43% against 51%.

ADP's dividend grew 12% a year from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2026, against 0.6% a year for IBM from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, and ADP carries far less debt.

At each dividend's current pace, ADP's income on $10,000 would pass IBM's in 2028, but ADP's stock costs 24x forward earnings to IBM's 19x.

Automatic Data Processing (ADP:NASDAQ) raised its quarterly dividend 12% to $1.90 a share on Nov. 11. That makes 52 consecutive years of increases.

International Business Machines (IBM:NYSE) has a different kind of record. Its board declared another $1.69 quarterly dividend on Oct. 21, and the company noted that "With payment of the December 10, 2026 dividend, IBM will have paid consecutive quarterly dividends every year since 1916."

Retirees seeking income want a check they can count on for decades. So which is the better dividend stock for retirees?

Source: TIKR, consensus estimates and company releases.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

IBM's dividend is safe, and barely growing

IBM covers its dividend comfortably. Over the twelve months to Sept. 30, it paid $6.34 billion in dividends out of $14.66 billion of free cash flow, a cash dividend payout ratio of 43%. Consensus puts that at a roomy 40% for fiscal 2026, and the company backs the improvement: on Oct. 21, it said it now expects full-year free cash flow to rise by more than $1 billion. Software led the third quarter, up 8%, with Red Hat up 11%.

The dividend has taken around half of free cash flow most years, with a high of 65.4% in fiscal 2022:

International Business Machines (IBM): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

The catch is growth. IBM paid $6.51 a share in fiscal 2020 and $6.71 in fiscal 2025, so $10,000 at its 2.7% yield pays $270 a year now and about $285 in year 10. That's a 2.9% yield on your original cash.

The bigger risk is debt: $63.8 billion at the end of the third quarter, IBM Financing included. And on Nov. 9, the EU's eu-LISA agency sued IBM, Atos and Leonardo over delays in rolling out the EU's border system. The agency says the case concerns only the development phase, so it doesn't change the cash math today.

title: Should You Buy HubSpot Stock For Its Cash?

Should You Buy HubSpot Stock For Its Cash?
Trefis Team

MSFT

Trading disclosure

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

HubSpot (HUBS) stock is worth a fresh look after falling 50.0% from its highest close of the past year of $405.83 on December 30, 2025. HubSpot's free cash flow over the last twelve months now equals 6.7% of its market value, against 4.2% for the median S&P 500 company. That yield marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink. So is HubSpot a business on sale, or a shrinking one?

HubSpot's Free Cash Flow Has Grown For Three Years

So far, HubSpot's cash profile resembles that of a business on sale. Its twelve-month free cash flow climbed from $243 million in the period ended September 2023 to $677 million in the period ended September 2026, and it was higher at every quarter end in between.

This matters to an owner. Shareholders own a slice of the free cash a business produces, whether paid out or not, just as they own a slice of its profit. When the market recognizes cash retained inside a company, the share price tends to follow, especially when that cash is growing.

HubSpot sells its software by subscription, and that software costs little to deliver: the company kept 83.0% of its revenue as gross profit over the last twelve months, against 77.3% at Salesforce. Its capital spending took 25.3% of the cash its operations brought in. HubSpot turned 18.9% of its revenue into free cash flow, against 17.3% at Microsoft. Three other peers turned more: 34.5% at Salesforce, 20.1% at IBM and 40.8% at Adobe.

Reported profit is thinner: HubSpot's operating margin was 5.4% over the last twelve months, up from a loss of 1.6% of revenue a year earlier. HubSpot's stock-based compensation over the same twelve months was $504 million, about 14% of its $3.59 billion of revenue. And HubSpot does not need its cash to pay down borrowing: at the end of September 2026 it held $1.30 billion of cash and short-term investments, against $224 million of debt.

Why Is HubSpot's Growth Slowing?

HubSpot's growth is slowing because customers are taking longer to buy, management said on the November 4, 2026 call. Revenue growth from a year earlier fell in the second and third quarters of 2026, from 23.4% in fiscal Q1 2026 to 19.8% in fiscal Q2 and 17.1% in fiscal Q3. Management expects growth of 12% for fiscal Q4 2026.

Management says customers are buying differently in the AI era. They want to test AI on their own data before they pay, and HubSpot's move to free trials and pricing tied to outcomes has lengthened buying cycles. Larger customers bring more decision-makers into each deal, while smaller ones are more sensitive to price.

What Happened With Rigetti Computing Stock Yesterday?

Rigetti Computing (RGTI) stock fell 8.6% yesterday, November 11, 2026, the first session after its Q3 FY2026 report, while the S&P 500 gained 1.3%. Its quantum peers moved less: IonQ fell 2.7%, while D-Wave Quantum rose 1.6%. Third-quarter revenue came in below the previous year's mark, but management still forecast about $20 million of revenue for full year 2026. So how much of that forecast is left for the fourth quarter?

What Rigetti Computing Needs From Its Fourth Quarter

About $9.1 million. Management said Rigetti booked $10.9 million of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, leaving the balance of the full-year forecast to the final three months. That requires bringing in almost as much in the last quarter as the company did over the previous nine months. The third quarter itself generated $1.41 million, down 27.5% from a year earlier.

Management said the full-year forecast assumes the C-DAC system passes customer acceptance in the fourth quarter, with the revenue recognized in that period. Rigetti is bringing that system up at C-DAC, India's national lab. So Rigetti's forecast is tied to that one delivery.

Is Rigetti Computing's Revenue Drop A One-Quarter Dip?

The drop looks more like one of Rigetti's sales swings than a new direction. Quarterly revenue rose to $4.40 million in Q1 FY2026 and $5.14 million in Q2 FY2026 before falling back in the third quarter. Management said quarterly revenue can vary meaningfully because it is tied to a small number of system deliveries, pointing to year-to-date revenue as the more useful view.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, revenue was $12.8 million, up 71% from a year earlier. That is still below the $14.7 million Rigetti reported for the twelve months to September 2023, so its sales have not yet risen steadily from one year to the next.

Rigetti Computing's Management On Sales And Spending

Management said quantum computing is still very much in the research and development phase. They noted that sales are not the right measure to follow until quantum advantage, the point where quantum computers pay off against classical ones. They also said the technology must be perfected before commercial sales can really take off. Management puts quantum advantage roughly three years away. When analysts asked about orders and backlog on the November 10 call, management pointed to growing interest from national labs, universities and a few commercial customers, but gave no figure.

How Risky Is Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock?

Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) lost 27.0% in the month to November 11, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 2.3%. The decline occurred between earnings reports. Over the same dates, Dell Technologies fell 34.6%. Although the shares are still up 114.2% over twelve months, the drop since October 13 shows how quickly the stock can give ground. So how far has Hewlett Packard Enterprise stock fallen when the whole market sold off?

HPE Stock Has Fallen Further Than The Market

During market shocks, HPE stock has usually dropped more than the S&P 500 before returning to its earlier high within months. The company has traded through 10 shocks since listing in November 2015, two of which share one 2015-16 fall. Across its 9 separate falls, the stock fell 23.6% on average, against 15.1% for the S&P 500.

The deepest decline in a market shock occurred during the 2020 COVID-19 crash, when HPE lost 45.3% and the index lost 33.7%. The 2025 US tariff shock came close, with the stock falling 42.3% against 18.8% for the S&P 500. The 2022 inflation shock was the only time HPE fell no further than the market: 23.9%, against 24.5% for the S&P 500.

The stock has also recovered every time. After each of the 9 falls, shares returned to their highest close before the low, taking a median of 4.2 months from the bottom. The slowest return followed the COVID-19 crash and took 10.6 months.

How Has Hewlett Packard Enterprise's Business Changed Since 2024?

Hewlett Packard Enterprise is a much bigger company than a year ago. It sold $41.9 billion over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, up 26.6% from a year earlier, and that is faster than the 14.0% growth of the twelve months before. These are reported figures; management's call figures are adjusted to include Juniper Networks, which HPE is integrating, from the start of fiscal 2025.

Profit has grown alongside sales. In fiscal Q3 2026, the GAAP operating margin reached 11.4%, compared with 2.7% in the same quarter of 2025.

HPE carries more debt than it did two years ago. Total debt stood at $20.2 billion on July 31, 2026, compared to $11.8 billion in July 2024, though the balance has declined from $23.7 billion a year earlier. That debt equals 30.2% of the company's market value, against 19.5% for the S&P 500.

Where Is Hewlett Packard Enterprise Under Pressure Now?

HPE has lacked the components necessary to meet demand. On the company's September 2, 2026 call, management said supply constraints continue to limit the volume of orders it can ship, and that memory chips such as DDR5 and NAND have been short since the beginning of 2026. Management said data center networking revenue declined 6% in fiscal Q3 on a normalized basis, which counts Juniper in both years, because of shipment timing driven by supply constraints.
